title: Green mosques
hook: mosques going solar and saving water

segments.voice: Yesterday, the environment, and Pickthall's word for the human role on the earth: viceroy. Your line was stewards, not owners. Which tap did you turn off sooner? Today, the stewardship comes home to one building. Day one thousand three hundred eighty-four.

A row of solar panels on a mosque roof, tilted toward the sun. There's a neat fit in that. The same sun already runs the building's day: dawn, noon, afternoon, sunset, nightfall, every prayer time set by where it sits in the sky. Now it lights the lamps too. And downstairs, in the washing area, someone has fitted taps that run slower, and piped the used water out to the garden. Today, green mosques, and the old reports that some Muslims point to behind them.
screen: `PANELS ON THE ROOF.` → `THE SUN SETS THE PRAYER TIMES.` → `WATER TO THE GARDEN.`

segments.voice: Start with the word mosque itself. The Arabic is masjid, a place of sajdah, of bowing the forehead to the ground. Then a hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari widens it. The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, lists things given to him, and one is this: the earth has been made for me a masjid and a means of purification. The whole earth, a place to pray. So a mosque building is, in a sense, a small roofed piece of a much larger mosque, and caring for the ground outside isn't a different job from caring for the carpet inside. Second, water. Before prayer comes wudu: washing the hands, face and arms, wiping the head, washing the feet. Anas reports in al-Bukhari that the Prophet did his wudu with a mudd, a small measure of water, and bathed with just a few of those measures. There's also a report in Sunan Ibn Majah, though its chain is debated, in which he sees a companion using a lot of water for wudu and asks what this excess is. The companion asks, can there be excess in wudu? And the answer comes back: yes, even if you are at a flowing river. Third, what that looks like now. Some mosques have put panels on their roofs. Some have swapped open taps for slower ones at the wudu stations, or collected the washing water to irrigate gardens. Some plant trees in the courtyard for shade. None of this is a new law. It's an old instinct, the earth as a place of prayer and water used with care, meeting new tools. And the place where it's easiest to see is the wudu tap.
screen: `MASJID: A PLACE OF BOWING.` · `THE WHOLE EARTH A MASJID.` · `WUDU WITH A MUDD OF WATER.` · `PANELS, SLOW TAPS, SHADE TREES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: learn about one place of worship, starting with one you know. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind a mosque, a church, a temple, a hall, any shared place where people gather. Walk through it slowly. The roof. The lights. The taps. The parking lot. The patch of ground out front. Notice where water runs, where power hums, where something could grow. Then pick one small thing you'd want to know: where its water goes, or whether anyone tends the garden. If you pray, you can hold the hadith in mind: the earth made a place of prayer. The bell holds the time.
Green mosques. Buildings that save power and water, drawing on a hadith that calls the whole earth a masjid, and on wudu done with a little water. Today's word.

Your line: mosques going green. Today, look up one mosque or place of worship near you and find one thing it does, or could do, with its roof, its water or its ground. Tomorrow, halal food today. Day one thousand three hundred eighty-four.

howItsDone: Some mosques install solar panels, fit water-saving taps at their wudu stations, or reuse washing water for gardens, and imams sometimes remind worshipers to use little water in wudu, following the Prophet's practice.

fork.setup: you're doing wudu beside a flowing river. there's endless water. is there such a thing as using too much?
options: no: it's a river, so it doesn't matter.
yes: even at a flowing river, says the report.
fork.reveal: in the report in Ibn Majah, whose chain is debated, the answer is yes, even at a flowing river. care with water doesn't depend on shortage.

original.note: Arabic: a mosque, a place of sajdah, bowing the forehead to the ground.

trapdoor: what you thought: a green mosque is a mosque painted green.
what it means: mosques that save power and water: solar panels, slower taps, reused wudu water, shade trees.
what a scholar hears: the hadith of the earth made a masjid in al-Bukhari, Anas's report of wudu with a mudd, and a debated report in Ibn Majah on excess even at a river.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 335 (the earth made a masjid and a means of purification)
Sahih al-Bukhari 201 (Anas: wudu with a mudd, bathing with a sa' up to five mudds)
Sunan Ibn Majah 425 (Sa'd at wudu: excess even at a flowing river)

notes: No specific green mosques are named and no figures are given, because none were sourced for this day. A Keeper may add a named, sourced example.
'Masjid, a place of sajdah': the link between masjid and sujud is standard, but confirm the phrasing; this is the only word-origin claim in the day.
Confirm hadith numbers: Bukhari 335, Bukhari 201, Ibn Majah 425. Ibn Majah 425 is widely graded weak (da'if); the script says 'its chain is debated'. Keeper may prefer 'graded weak'.

'Dawn, noon, afternoon, sunset, nightfall, every prayer time set by where it sits in the sky': confirm the description of the five prayer times by the sun is acceptable (Isha is set by the end of twilight).
Wudu is summarized as hands, face, arms, wiping the head, and feet; the full form also includes rinsing mouth and nose. Confirm the simplification.

Editor: 'bathed with not much more' understated Anas's report (a sa' up to five mudds), so it now says 'just a few of those measures' in the teach and the myth reveal; added wiping the head to the wudu summary; replaced the hook's 'less like a trend and more like a homecoming' with a plain line.
